MlxOSBrix.NativeFirst: brixOS may use its own handle, wait, memory-map, process and IPC primitives.
MlxOSBrix.PosixFacade: std.posix translates required POSIX semantics onto brixOS native primitives.
MlxOSBrix.WaylandTransport: brixOS must provide a Wayland-capable byte-stream transport with ancillary handle/fd passing semantics, shared memory object export/import, and poll/wait integration. The public Mlx Wayland API remains identical across Linux, BSD and brixOS.

Principles.Rule: Every kernel resource a process uses is an object it holds by a handle; nothing is reached by a global number (a pid, a signal number, a descriptor number) without a handle.
There is one way to wait: for any of a set of handles to reach a state, with a deadline.
The kernel keeps no hidden cursor: a read or write names its position, or says it streams.

A process learns of what happens to it (an interrupt from its terminal, a child that ended, a fault) as events it takes from its own queue; code runs asynchronously only through the one upcall the process registers.
Copy on write is the system's way to copy: files, trees (snapshots), volumes and processes (branch) are copied by sharing pages.

The Linux system call numbers are served by a separate layer of the kernel (its own number space) that translates them onto these objects; nothing in the kernel's core names a Linux number, structure or signal.

CallingConvention.Rule: SYSCALL with the call number in rax, at or above NATIVE_BASE (0x4000); the arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9.
The result in rax: a value (zero or more), or a negative Status.
Numbers below NATIVE_BASE are Linux's (the translation layer). A process may use both while std moves over.

Status.note: returned negated; std turns them into Mlx error sets
Status.Code: the handle's object does not do that
the other end of a stream or channel is closed
the upcall ran during the call
a table is full (handles of a process)
too many links on the way
a link or rename across volumes

what a socket was to send cannot leave this machine as it is: it has no network device, the link is down, it has no address, or the destination is not on its subnet and there is no gateway (the link's record says which)

Handles.Rule: A handle is a non-zero 32-bit value naming an entry of the process's handle table: an object and the rights the entry carries. 0 is no handle.
A handle names the entry as it was when the handle was made (its generation): once closed, the handle stays invalid even when the entry is used again.
Rights only shrink: duplicate gives the same object with a subset of the rights; a handle sent over a channel moves with its rights.
Handles.Rights: read write wait duplicate transfer control
Handles.Kinds: process group node stream channel session memory timer socket

States.note: a 32-bit word per object; wait watches it
States.Bit: a read would not block (a stream or channel has data, a node, a session with input for its front group, a timer that expired)
a process ended; a group has no process left
a process has a change to take (a child ended, stopped or went on)
a process has events in its queue
a group: it is in front of the session

Wait.WaitItem: handle: u32, want: u32 (state bits), seen: u32 (written: the state when the call returned), reserved: u32
Wait.Rule: The call returns as soon as one item's state has a wanted bit, with every item's seen word filled; 0 and timed_out when the deadline (monotonic nanoseconds, 0: do not block, all ones: none) passes first.
A process waiting is woken by the state change itself; nothing polls.

handle_info(h, info*) -> kind (info: kind, rights, state)
wait(items, count, deadline) -> ready
read(h, buffer, length, at) -> count (at: a byte position, or STREAM = all ones for streams, sessions and channels)
write(h, buffer, length, at) -> count
node_open(directory h, path, length, flags, mode) -> h (directory 0: the process's working directory; flags: read 1, write 2, create 4, exclusive 8, truncate 16)
node_info(h, info*) (kind 1 file, 2 directory, 3 link, 4 fifo, 5 device; mode, links: u32; reserved: u32; size, modified in nanoseconds since 1970, the node's number: u64)
node_make(directory h, path, length, kind | mode << 8, target, target length) (kind: 2 directory, 4 fifo, 3 link to target)
node_remove(directory h, path, length)
node_rename(directory h, path, length, directory h, path, length)
node_list(h, buffer, length, cookie) -> bytes (entries: kind, name length, name; the cookie to go on)
stream_pair(handles*, flags) (a pipe: two ends; flags: close on replace 1)
channel_pair(handles*) (messages with handles)
channel_send(h, bytes, length, handles*, count)
channel_receive(h, bytes, capacity, handles*, capacity, sizes*)

memory_unmap(address, size)

memory_map_object(h, offset, size, flags) -> address (flags: write 1, which needs the handle's write right; the pages are shared by every mapping, a branch keeps them shared, they outlive the handle while mapped)

process_spawn(program h, start block, handles*, count) -> process h (the start block: arguments, environment, roles*, role count, one word each; a role record: role u32, handle u32, the handle one of the handles given; no roles: input, output and errors are the first three)
process_branch() -> process h in the parent, 0 in the child (a copy-on-write copy of the caller)
process_replace(program h, start block) (the caller runs another program; handles marked close-on-exec by the Linux layer, and every process and group handle, are closed)
process_exit(code)
process_change(h, change*) -> 0 or would_block (takes a child's change: what (1 exited, 2 ended by an event, 3 stopped, 4 went on), the code or the event's kind, its detail, reserved: u32 each)
event_send(process or group h, kind) (a group: every process in it; not_found when none is)
events_claim(kinds) (the kinds the program handles itself)
events_take(records*, count) -> taken
upcall_set(entry, stack, size)
upcall_return(context*)
group_join(process h or 0 for the caller (else one of its children), group h or 0 for a new one numbered as the process) -> group h (state: front, ended when no process is in it)
session_front(session h, group h) (the group gets the session's interrupt, quit and suspend events and may read it)
clock_read(clock) -> nanoseconds (0 monotonic, 1 real time)

timer_create(deadline, period) -> h (deadline on the monotonic clock, period 0: once; readable once it expired; a streaming read of 8 bytes takes how many times it expired since the last read, waiting for the deadline; 0 bytes when it will not expire again)

snapshot(source directory h, directory h, path, length, flags) (a copy of the tree the handle names at path, its files sharing their pages; flags: read-only 1; the disk's volume into /volumes is a snapshot on the disk, read-only only)
handle_of_descriptor(descriptor) -> h (the handle of a descriptor the Linux layer opened; for std while it moves over)
directory_set(directory h) (the working directory, which a 0 directory handle names)
node_path(directory h or 0, buffer, capacity) -> length (its path, NUL-terminated; too_large when it does not fit)
node_map(file h, offset, size) -> address (the file's pages mapped as the caller's, shared until a write copies one: a private view; the file does not change)

socket_open(kind) -> h (a socket: stream 1 (TCP), datagram 2 (UDP), ping 3 (ICMP echo: the echo requests sent are given the socket's identifier; it receives their replies and, as they came, ICMP's messages that one of them was not delivered: a router's or a host's, and the system's own "destination unreachable, host unreachable" from this machine's address, made in the same form, when a request waited for the hardware address of its neighbour (the host, or the gateway to it) and nobody said it); kind socket; a machine without a network device has sockets all the same: they reach the machine itself, 127.0.0.0/8)
socket_bind(socket h, port) (0: one the system picks)

socket_connect(socket h, address*) (address: 4 bytes IPv4, port u32; a stream's connection begins: WRITABLE when made, PEER_GONE when it failed; unreachable, at once and with nothing begun, when nothing can leave this machine for the address as things are; invalid for a stream when the address is no one host's: everyone's (255.255.255.255, the subnet's last address) or a group's (224.0.0.0 and above); a datagram socket's peer)

socket_listen(socket h) (connections asked of it are made by the system and wait to be accepted, 16 at the most: while that many wait, one that is asked gets no answer, and its peer asks again; what is asked and not yet made, the peer's answer to the system's being awaited, takes no socket, is given up after 7 seconds, and gives way to a newer one when the system holds 64 of them)
socket_accept(socket h, peer* or 0) -> h (would_block: none yet; the listener is READABLE when one waits)

socket_send(socket h, data, length, address* or 0) -> count (would_block: none taken; a datagram's destination, or the peer; a ping socket's destination is the address alone, its port unused; a datagram to a neighbour whose hardware address is not known yet is taken: the system keeps it while it asks, under a second, and sends it when the answer comes; unreachable: a datagram or an echo request cannot leave this machine as it is, said at once; would_block for a datagram also says the device is busy now; a datagram to 255.255.255.255 or to the subnet's last address goes to everyone on the wire, to everyone's hardware address)
socket_receive(socket h, data, capacity, from* or 0) -> count (0: the peer closed; would_block: nothing yet)
socket_info(socket h, into*) (local address, peer address, the pending error (a Status code, taken), connected)

session_pair(handles*) -> 0 (a terminal of its own: handles[0] its control side, a stream: what programs write to the session is read there, what is written there is typed; handles[1] the session, kind session, for the programs; the control side's reads wait for output, its state READABLE when there is some)
session_size(session or control h, columns, rows) (the terminal's size in cells, what the window size asked by TIOCGWINSZ is)
system_power(kind) -> (does not return; no_right unless the caller is the first process) (every volume committed, then the machine halted (0), powered off (1) or restarted (2))

system_info(buffer, capacity) -> count (the machine's figures as words: memory bytes, free bytes, processors, uptime ns, page faults served, system calls, switches between processes, the devices' message-signalled interrupts taken, then the waits for the kernel in ns: those of processors that had something to run summed, the longest since the boot, what held the kernel for most of it (the process id above 32 bits, 0 for a processor that idled; below, 0x80000000 and a system call's number, an interrupt's or fault's vector, or 0x7FFFFFFF for the idle loop), the longest of the last ten to twenty seconds and its holder, the waits of processors with nothing to run summed; how many there are, the first `capacity` written)
identity_set(user, group) (the caller's identity, which its children inherit; a process of user 0 may take any, another only its own: no_right)
node_own(h, user, group) (the node's owner and group, all ones: as it is; user 0 may give a node away, its owner may change its group alone)

channel_peer(channel h, into*) (who holds the other end: the process that made or opened it, pid, user, group, name length (u32 each), then its program's leaf name up to 64 bytes; a bus learns a client's identity and app so)

volume_info(directory h or 0, path, length, buffer, capacity, flags) -> count (the volume the path is on, as words: its kind (0 the tree's own, in memory; 1 a brixfs volume of a disk), a block's bytes, blocks, free blocks (a count the store keeps, no walk over the disk's map), inodes at the most, inode numbers never used, its generation, 1 when read-only, 1 when a commit frees just what it replaced (0: the free blocks are found by a walk over every root after each), then what the store did since the mount: the mount's nanoseconds, commits, the last and the longest commit's nanoseconds, walks over every root, the last walk's nanoseconds, blocks read, blocks written; flags: check 1 (user 0 only, no_right else): what changed is committed, the free blocks are found again by a walk over every root and compared with what the store held: the blocks it held that no root reaches, the blocks a root reaches that it did not hold (0 unless the store is at fault); how many words there are, the first `capacity` written)

listener_make(directory h, path, length, mode) -> h (a listener node: opening it gives the opener a channel of its own and sends its far end to this handle as a message with no bytes and one handle; would_block when the listener has not taken the earlier ones, peer_gone when its end is closed; the node goes with node_remove)

process_start(records*, capacity) -> count (the caller's handles by role, as (role u32, handle u32) records: input 1, output 2, errors 3, directory 4 (its working directory at the start), session 5, a spawner's own from 16; the count of them all, the first `capacity` written)

Events.Rule: An event is a record (kind, sender's process id, detail) in the receiving process's queue; its state has the events bit while the queue is not empty.
Events.Kind: Ctrl-Z at the session, or a request
a stopped process goes on; always also done
a child has a change to take
detail: the fault and its address; delivered at once, through the upcall only
the process read its session from a group that is not in front
the session's size changed, urgent data
one the program and its senders give a meaning (the detail)
a write to a stream whose reader is gone
Events.Rule: events_take writes records of four u32: kind, detail, sender (a process id; 0 the kernel), reserved (a fault: the low half of its address).

A process that has claimed no kind and set no upcall sees its events through the Linux layer's view (signals), as the programs built for Linux expect; one that has, sees them as events. A fault such a process has not claimed still goes to a handler it has in the Linux layer's view for the fault's signal (a crash report installed there stays the program's when it claims other kinds).
An event kind the program has not claimed takes its default. A claimed one stays in the queue for the program; with an upcall set, the kernel runs it.

The upcall: the interrupted registers and SSE state are saved in a context record on the upcall's stack, entry(context*) runs, upcall_return(context*) goes back. No second upcall starts before the first returns; a call the upcall interrupted returns interrupted.
There are no per-kind handlers, masks or numbers in the kernel: std.posix builds sigaction, sigprocmask and signal numbers on the queue and the one upcall.

Processes.Rule: A program starts with a start block: its arguments, its environment and its handles by role (input, output, errors, working directory, session, and any the spawner adds). The arguments and environment are on its stack; process_start gives the roles, which a branch copies and a replace's start block sets anew.
process_spawn starts a program in a new process with exactly the handles given. process_branch copies the caller (copy on write, as snapshots copy trees); std.posix's fork is a branch.

The first process is /system/programs/impulse when the archive has it (else flux), with the serial console as its input, output, errors and session; it alone may call system_power. It starts the services of /system/settings/init/services with process_spawn and roles, answers impulsectl on the FIFO /temporary/init/control, and shows the boot on a display with ignition on two streams.

All of the machine's memory is the kernel's to hand out (mapped at its start beyond the GiB the boot tables map); system_info says how much there is and is free, with the processors, the uptime and the kernel's counts, for a program that sizes its work by them (std.build's runner).
The mouse is /devices/mouse: the PS/2 mouse's bytes as they come (three a packet, the first with bit 3 set), a read waiting for them.

The display is /devices/framebuffer: a read gives its geometry (ten words: width, height, bytes a row, format, the shape of the screen it is shown on as a width and a height, the display's number, how many displays there are, and the PCI vendor and device of the adapter whose memory its picture is in, 0 and 0 when that is not known; a read of fewer bytes gives the first of them, 32 the four words of the picture, 48 those and the shape), node_map its pixels (32 bits each, blue first; red first when the format says 2). The shape is the monitor's own mode when the firmware passes on what the monitor says, else the mode the boot image names, else the picture's own size. Where it is another shape than the picture's, the monitor is taken to stretch the picture across the screen (the kernel cannot see whether it does, or shows the picture in its own shape with borders), and a program that wants a circle round on the screen draws for that shape. The keyboard is /devices/keyboard: its scancodes (set 1) as they come, a read waiting for them. A virtual console is a program on both with a session pair (mlx-console).

A machine may have several displays (a graphics adapter on the board and one in a slot, a monitor on each): every graphics output of the firmware that has a picture of its own in memory the kernel can write is one, eight at most. The kernel numbers them from 0 in the firmware's order and says each in its log (size, memory, adapter, node). One is the main display, /devices/framebuffer: the one the boot image's settings/display names (a line "main N", N the display's number, or "main VVVV:DDDD", its adapter's PCI vendor and device in hex), else the one whose monitor names the largest mode of its own, else the one with the largest picture, of several alike the firmware's first. The others are /devices/framebuffer1, /devices/framebuffer2 and on, in their order, without gaps: the same record to read (with their own number, and the same count), the same pixels to map, each in its own size and format. A machine with one display has no /devices/framebuffer1. The kernel's console is on every display until a program maps that display's node. A program that draws on the screen itself shows the main display's picture on the others too, fitted to each one's size without distortion: as large as it goes in the shape it was drawn in (its pixels square, on a screen that stretches a display's picture too), in the middle, black beside it (std.displays: what changed is brought, in a bounded part of a frame's time); a program that knows of one display draws on the main one, and the others keep what they showed.

A network link is /devices/netN (net0 the first, numbered from 0 without gaps; a machine without a network device has none): a read at a position gives its record (NetworkLink) as things are at that moment (a streaming read goes through it once), and nothing is written to it (wrong_kind); node_info says a device whose size is the record's bytes, and everyone may read it. The kernel runs the network (the device, DHCP or the settings file /system/settings/network, the stack); a program reads a link's state here and reaches the network through sockets. 127.0.0.0/8 is the machine itself: what a socket sends there comes back in without a network device, a link, an address or a frame on the wire, from the address it was sent to. What is sent to everyone (255.255.255.255, or the subnet's last address) is taken by datagram sockets alone: a stream's segment or an echo request addressed so is not answered.

A group is an object: processes join it; a session (a terminal) has a front group, which gets its interrupt, quit and suspend events and may read it. A streaming read of the session from a group behind sends that group read_behind and waits (the processes stop and read again when they go on); io_error when the event would not reach the reader.

NetworkLink.note: the record a read of /devices/netN gives: 72 bytes, little-endian, the addresses in network order
NetworkLink.Field: the record's bytes as this kernel has it (72; 64 before the lease's fields); a later kernel's is longer, its new fields after these: a program reads what it knows of it, and one that asks for fewer bytes gets the record's first
0x1: the link is up (a cable with a partner at its other end); 0x2: DHCP is asking for an address (there is none)
where the address is from: 0 nowhere (there is none: the four addresses are 0.0.0.0, and nothing is sent or answered but DHCP's own messages), 1 DHCP, 2 the settings file
megabits a second; 0 when the device does not say or the link is down
the hardware address, two bytes of 0 after it
the driver's name, 0 after its end (virtio, igb)
0.0.0.0: none (the configuration came without one: only the own subnet is reached)
the frames the device took since the boot
the frames given to it to send (with the link down none is given to it: what was to go is dropped, and a socket's send says unreachable)
the seconds DHCP's lease still runs; 0: there is no lease (a static configuration, or no address); 0xFFFFFFFF: it does not end
the seconds the lease was given for, with the same two special values
NetworkLink.Rule: The settings file has a line each for address, netmask, gateway and nameserver (a name, a blank, a.b.c.d); it is read once, at boot. With an address line the configuration is static and DHCP does not run: a gateway or a name server the file has no line for is none, a netmask it has no line for is the one of the address's class. Without an address line (0.0.0.0 on it is none) nothing of the file is used and DHCP asks, and goes on asking (after 1, 2, 4, 8 and then every 16 seconds, and at once when the link comes up) until it is answered. A netmask line that is no netmask (a one bit behind a zero bit, or 0.0.0.0) makes the file unusable in the same way: the kernel's log says so, nothing of the file is used, and DHCP asks.

DHCP's answer is the configuration: a router or a name server it leaves out is none. The kernel renews the lease on its own (RFC 2131: of its server from half of the lease's time, of everyone from seven eighths, or at the times the server names); when the lease ends unrenewed, or a server refuses it, there is no address again (configured 0, DHCP asking) until DHCP is answered anew. A netmask in the answer that is none is taken as none given (the address's class's).

The kernel looks at the link on every tick of its timer. When it goes down or comes up the kernel's log has a line ("net0: the link is down"; "net0: the link is up, 1000 Mbit/s full duplex", without the speed where the device does not say it, and with the number of frames that were not sent while it was down when there were some). While it is down nothing is given to the device. When it comes up, what was known of the neighbours' hardware addresses is forgotten and DHCP begins again: where it is asking, its next question goes at once; where it holds an address, the lease is asked for anew at once, of everyone (again after 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds while nobody answers, then at the lease's own pace): its server's answer renews it, a server's refusal gives the address up, and with no answer the address is kept until the lease ends. At boot a link that is not up yet is waited for, half a second at the most.

Personality.Rule: A process has an identity, a user and a group: the first process's is 0, spawn and branch pass it on, replace keeps it, identity_set changes it (down from 0 for good). A node has an owner and a group (node_make gives the maker's; node_own changes them) and a mode, which decide what a process may do with it; user 0 may do anything. The login (sentinel) branches, takes the person's identity and replaces itself with their session; the accounts are /system/settings/users, groups and shadow.

The Linux layer (kernel/linux) takes the numbers below NATIVE_BASE: descriptors are its view of handles, signals its view of events (SIGINT the interrupt event, SIGTSTP suspend, SIGCHLD child, rt_sigframes its view of the upcall), errno its view of Status.
